title: Certifying Concept Unlearning in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning
  [Submitted on 10 Sep 2026]
    Title:Certifying Concept Unlearning in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Existing evaluations of concept unlearning in text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models primarily rely on attack success rates obtained through automated adversarial prompt search. However, these metrics provide only empirical evidence over a finite set of queries and leave residual leakage over the broader prompt space largely unquantified. This limitation can lead to overestimating unlearning effectiveness and underestimating safety risks. To address this gap, we introduce a novel certification framework for T2I concept unlearning that provides high-confidence guarantees with bounded error on residual concept leakage. Our approach combines statistical certification with worst-case analysis along concept-relevant embedding directions to derive explicit upper bounds on leakage probability under user-specified confidence levels. We evaluate our framework across three major concept categories namely NSFW content, artistic styles, and celebrity identities, and six state-of-the-art unlearning methods. Certified leakage bounds consistently exceed standard attack success rates by 16.2%, uncovering substantial residual risks missed by existing evaluation protocols. Crucially, our results demonstrate that empirical attack-based evaluations can significantly underestimate residual leakage and establish certification as a necessary complement for reliable auditing of concept unlearning in T2I diffusion models.

report.summary: New certification framework shows attack-based evaluations underestimate residual concept leakage in text-to-image diffusion unlearning by 16.2% across NSFW, style, and celebrity concepts.
report.background: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate harmful, copyrighted, or identity-specific content, prompting concept unlearning methods that aim to erase NSFW material, artistic styles, or celebrity identities from model weights. Current evaluations typically measure attack success rates found by automated adversarial prompt search: they query a finite set of prompts and report how often the target concept appears. This gives only empirical evidence and leaves residual leakage across the much broader prompt space largely unquantified, which can overstate unlearning effectiveness and understate safety risks. The paper introduces a certification framework that combines statistical certification with worst-case analysis along concept-relevant embedding directions to produce explicit, high-confidence upper bounds on leakage probability. It evaluates NSFW content, artistic styles, and celebrity identities across six state-of-the-art unlearning methods.
key_points: Existing evaluations rely on attack success rates from automated adversarial prompt search. Because these tests cover only a finite query set, they cannot quantify leakage over the full prompt space, so they may overestimate how completely a concept has been removed from a text-to-image diffusion model.

The proposed certification framework blends statistical certification with worst-case analysis along concept-relevant embedding directions. It derives explicit upper bounds on residual leakage probability under user-specified confidence, turning unlearning auditing from empirical spot-checking into a bounded-error guarantee.

Across three concept categories—NSFW content, artistic styles, and celebrity identities—and six state-of-the-art unlearning methods, certified leakage bounds exceeded standard attack success rates by 16.2%. This gap indicates substantial residual risk that ordinary evaluations miss.

The results show empirical attack-based evaluations can significantly underestimate leakage. Certification should therefore complement, not replace, attack testing, giving model providers and auditors a more reliable way to verify concept unlearning before deployment.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this work challenges unlearning claims that rely only on attack success rates and points toward certified audits as a compliance and safety standard. Model providers may need to report leakage bounds, retain stronger safety layers, and accept that some concepts remain partially recoverable. Developers get a new evaluation target: worst-case leakage along concept-relevant embedding directions, not just a checklist of adversarial prompts. This could inspire open-source certification tooling and benchmark suites. For regular users, better auditing means stronger protection against NSFW, celebrity, or style misuse, but also potentially stricter filters, reduced creative flexibility, and slower releases as teams address residual risks before shipping.
report.tools: To follow up, watch the paper's eventual code release on arXiv or GitHub. Relevant open-source tools include Hugging Face Diffusers for T2I pipelines and safety checkers, PyTorch for embedding-direction analysis, and unlearning baselines such as ESD, UCE, SLD, and Concept Ablation. Detection libraries like NudeNet or CLIP-based classifiers can operationalize concept leakage checks, while adversarial prompt search frameworks help compare empirical attack success rates against certified bounds.
